counterfactuals.reason: The failure mechanism is that VFIO passthrough requires exclusive device ownership - the discrete GPU cannot be simultaneously bound to both host driver and vfio-pci for guest access. The proposed change directly addresses this by providing three alternative architectures that enable concurrent access: (1) SR-IOV/vGPU creates multiple virtual GPU instances from one physical device, allowing separate bindings for host and guest simultaneously, (2) GPU multiplexing/time-slicing at hypervisor level manages shared access without exclusive binding, or (3) dual-GPU configuration eliminates the constraint entirely by giving host the integrated GPU while guest gets the discrete GPU. Each mechanism breaks the single-owner binding model that causes the failure. With any of these implementations, the user would no longer face the binary choice between host GPU access and VM GPU acceleration.

The proposed GPU virtualization capability directly addresses the exclusive hardware ownership problem. With either SR-IOV or hypervisor-mediated GPU sharing, the single physical GPU can present multiple virtual GPU instances - one bound to the Linux host driver and one passed to the Windows guest. This eliminates the mutual exclusivity that prevents simultaneous host access. The device emulation layer that multiplexes access specifically resolves the current inability to time-slice or share GPU resources between host and guest. While Windows 11's WDDM 3.x overhead would still exist within the guest, the fundamental failure mechanism - inability to access Linux host GPU while VM runs due to exclusive VFIO passthrough - would be completely removed by enabling concurrent virtualized GPU access for both host and guest.

counterfactuals.reason: The failure occurs because the overlay filesystem manager enters an unconfigured state intermittently, causing checkpoint operations to fail. The proposed change directly addresses this by initializing and verifying the overlay manager configuration state before accepting checkpoint recovery commands. This prevents checkpoint listing (which fails with HTTP 500 when the manager is unconfigured) and restoration attempts (which fail with missing files due to unresolved paths from missing manager configuration) from executing when the manager is in an unconfigured state. By ensuring the manager is properly configured before any checkpoint operations proceed, the bidirectional absence problem—where the manager configuration is absent when needed and filesystem objects cannot be resolved—is eliminated at the root cause.

The failure mechanism is that checkpoint recovery operations are invoked when the overlay filesystem manager is not initialized or configured, causing the system to have checkpoint metadata but no mechanism to resolve logical references to physical storage paths. The proposed change directly addresses this by verifying the overlay filesystem manager is configured and checkpoint file paths are resolvable BEFORE accepting restart/wake commands, and queuing commands during unconfigured states until configuration is confirmed. This prevents the exact causal sequence: recovery commands would no longer be executed against an unconfigured overlay manager, eliminating the HTTP 500 'overlay manager not configured' error and the cascading path resolution failures. The intermittency would also be eliminated because commands would wait for proper configuration rather than racing against variable initialization timing.

counterfactuals.reason: The failure occurred because scale-down depended entirely on manual human action from a specific workstation, with no automated trigger, monitoring, or alerts. The proposed change attaches termination conditions directly to machines at creation time (maximum lifetime timeout, dependency on batch job process ID, or API-based lifecycle hook), making cleanup execute independently of the management workstation's continued existence. This eliminates the dependency on human memory, the specific workstation, and manual command execution. With termination conditions attached at creation (e.g., timeout after job completion or when batch process ends), the 40 idle machines would have automatically terminated after the batch jobs completed, preventing the two-week run and $600 cost regardless of workstation retirement.

The proposed change implements automated scale-down that triggers upon batch job completion signal, independent of manual intervention or specific workstation availability. This directly addresses all three causal factors in the failure: (1) it eliminates dependency on manual cleanup execution, (2) it removes dependency on the specific workstation that was destroyed, and (3) it establishes autonomous termination logic linked to batch job lifecycle. With this change fully in place, the temporary machines would automatically terminate when the batch job completes, regardless of whether the management workstation still exists. The failure mechanism—elimination of the only carrier of termination function combined with absence of autonomous termination logic—would no longer exist.
